Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

trick noun

something done to deceive

also a trick, tricks, dirty trick, ruse, deception, is this a trick?, bamboozle, you bamboozled me, fool someone, take someone in, dupe, you’ve been duped, there’s a catch, there’s a catch to it, cheat, screw (cheat), take someone for a sucker

classical

Caes. B.G. 1.13.6: magis virtūte … quam dolō
Traupman 398

dolus, dolī m.

noun, second declension · Declension on Wiktionary

a trick, guile

Any trick or ruse; the plural dolī are the schemes of comedy’s slaves. In law, dolus malus is fraud. “Play fair” is “without tricks”: sine dolō.

Other words

  • fallācia, fallāciae f. — a trick, a deception, an intrigue

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Ter. And. 212: faciam in nūptiīs fallāciam; Cic. Att. 1.1.1: sine fūcō ac fallāciīs (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    In Cicero only plural (Lewis & Short).

  • techna, technae f. — a trick, a dodge

    noun, first declension · also used · classical · Plaut. Capt. 3.4.109; Ter. Eun. 4.4.51 (Lewis & Short) · Declension on Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.)

    From Greek τέχνη; “ante-classical” in Lewis & Short, that is, the comedians’ word.

  • captiō, captiōnis f. — a catch, a trick (in words or in a deal)

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Traupman 110: num hoc est captiō?; Cic. Quint. 53 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 398 · Declension on Wiktionary

  • verba dare (alicui) — fool, cheat, take someone in

    also used · classical · Ter. And. 1.3.6: cui verba dare difficile est (Lewis & Short s.v. verbum); Traupman 93

    Literally “to give someone (mere) words”.

  • ōs sublinere (alicui) — make a fool of, bamboozle

    also used · classical · Plaut. Merc. 3.4.19: pulchrē ōs sublēvit patrī (Lewis & Short s.v. sublinō); Traupman 97

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut.)

    Literally “to smear someone’s face”, from the prank played on a sleeper (Lewis & Short).

  • dēfraudō, dēfraudāre, dēfraudāvī, dēfraudātum — cheat someone (out of something)

    verb, first conjugation · also used · classical · Plaut. Asin. 1.1.81 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 375 · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    (vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; in ōrātiōne solūtā rāra)

    Lewis & Short: ante-classical and late; Cicero uses it twice, only in proverbial phrases. Classical prose says fraudāre.

Examples

  • dolus an virtūs, quis in hoste requīrat?

    trickery or courage: who would ask which, against an enemy?Verg. A. 2.390

  • nam dolī nōn dolī sunt, nisi astū colās

    for tricks aren’t tricks unless you work them cleverlyPlaut. Capt. 2.1.30

  • Lūditō lēgitimē, absque technīs ac dolō malō.

    Play fair, without tricks or cheating.Erasm. Coll., Lūsus puerīlēs

  • Enim istaec captiō est.

    This is clearly a trick.Plaut. Ep. 5.2.36 (Lewis & Short)

  • Mihi dedistī verba.

    You bamboozled me.Traupman 93

  • Tibi ōs est sublitum plānē et probē.

    You’ve been duped good and proper.Traupman 97

See also trick, magic trick, lie, playful.
